summary:
We developed Soil Time Machine, a bilingual web app that helps farmers compare how different crop rotations could affect the same field over three to five years. Farmers can map their field, enter their current rotation, and test alternatives under hotter, drier, or wetter conditions. The app combines NASA weather and satellite data with soil estimates and farmer inputs to compare irrigation demand, water stress, crop suitability, and changes in soil organic carbon. An interactive demo shows how it works for a rice-growing field in Thới Lai, Cần Thơ, Vietnam.

The project addresses the challenge of turning Earth observation data into practical planting decisions. A farmer considering replacing a rice crop with a legume, for example, can explore what that change could mean for water demand and soil carbon before committing a season. The app labels observations and model estimates so farmers can weigh the trade-offs with a clear view of the evidence.
details:
How it works

We built Soil Time Machine for farmers who want to see how changing what they plant could affect their fields over three to five years. Farmers locate a field on a map, enter their current crop rotation and water availability, and compare that rotation with alternatives under historical, hotter, drier, or wetter conditions. The app combines NASA POWER weather data and satellite products with SoilGrids estimates and farmer inputs. It uses FAO-56 methods to estimate irrigation demand and the RothC model to estimate changes in soil organic carbon.

What makes it creative and why it matters

The app lets farmers explore several possible futures for the same field. A rice grower in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta can test what might happen if they replace a dry-season rice crop with a legume, then see how estimated irrigation demand, crop suitability, and soil carbon change together. Farmers can adjust how much each outcome matters to them, see why a plan ranks higher, and turn their chosen rotation into a printable planting calendar. Our goal is to help farmers anticipate water shortfalls and weigh soil health alongside seasonal planting decisions.

What we considered

We designed around Mekong Delta planting seasons, including the effects of salinity, drainage, and seasonal water availability. The app supports English and Vietnamese, works on phones and computers, and offers table views for charts. Regional data can miss conditions within a field, so we show the source and scale of the data, label model estimates, and give priority to farmer-provided soil measurements. Soil carbon estimates still need local field validation.

Tools we used

We built the browser app in TypeScript with React, Next.js, and Tailwind CSS. We used MapLibre GL for interactive maps, Recharts for charts, and Vercel to host the demo. Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with parts of the code and documentation, which the team reviewed and tested.
